prompt:
Write a narrative account of about 1,200 words of the Apollo 13 accident and the crew's return to Earth. The reader is a general reader.

Do not use dashes, semicolons, colons or parentheses.

text:
On the afternoon of April 11, 1970, a Saturn V rocket lifted off from Kennedy Space Center carrying three men toward the Moon. Apollo 13 was meant to be the third lunar landing. By then the public had grown a little bored with the whole business. Two crews had already walked on the Moon, and television networks had stopped carrying the flights live. That indifference would not last the week.

The crew was James Lovell, Fred Haise and Jack Swigert. Lovell was the veteran, a Navy man on his fourth spaceflight and the commander of the mission. Haise was a rookie who would pilot the lunar module. Swigert had only joined the crew days before launch. The original command module pilot, Ken Mattingly, had been exposed to German measles and was grounded by the flight surgeons, so Swigert stepped in after a frantic few days of training. Lovell named the command module Odyssey. The lunar module was called Aquarius.

The first two days were almost dull. The spacecraft coasted outward, the crew ate, slept and sent home a television broadcast, and the controllers in Houston dealt with a few small glitches. Then, on the evening of April 13, about 200,000 miles from Earth, Mission Control asked the crew to stir the tanks of supercold oxygen and hydrogen that fed the ship. Stirring kept the contents from stratifying, and it made the gauges more accurate. Swigert flipped the switch.

Moments later there was a bang, and the ship shuddered. Warning lights lit up across the panel. Swigert radioed Houston, and Lovell followed with the sentence that became famous in a slightly altered form. He said, "Houston, we've had a problem."

What had happened was a quiet disaster years in the making. The oxygen tank had been damaged on the ground before the flight. During a test, technicians had struggled to drain it and had left its heaters running at a voltage far higher than the tank was designed for. That cooked the Teflon insulation on the wires inside. When Swigert turned on the stirring fans, a spark in the ruined wiring ignited the insulation in a tank full of pure oxygen. The tank burst, and the blast tore off a panel of the service module and crippled the second oxygen tank beside it.

The oxygen supplied the fuel cells that made the ship's electricity and also the water and the air the men breathed. Within minutes the crew could see the second tank draining. Haise and Lovell watched the pressure fall. Looking out the window, Lovell saw gas venting into space, a pale cloud streaming away from the ship. It was clear that the Moon was no longer the goal. The goal was to get home.

In Houston, flight director Gene Kranz gathered his teams and set them to work. The command module Odyssey was dying, and its batteries had to be saved for the final descent through the atmosphere. The only place with power, oxygen and water to spare was Aquarius, the lunar module, which had been built to carry two men for about two days. Now it had to keep three men alive for four. The crew climbed into the little lander and used it as a lifeboat.

The next question was the trajectory. The ship was on a path that would swing it around the Moon, but it was not aimed at Earth. Engineers considered turning around at once, but that would have required using the damaged service module engine, which nobody trusted. They chose to fly around the Moon and use the lander's descent engine to speed the return. After the ship had looped behind the far side and come out the other side, Lovell and Haise fired Aquarius for a long burn to shorten the trip home. On the way around, the men passed farther from Earth than any humans had ever travelled, nearly 250,000 miles. They had little time to appreciate it.

The days that followed were a test of endurance. Aquarius was shut down to the barest minimum of power, which meant the cabin grew bitterly cold. The temperature dropped to around 40 degrees Fahrenheit, and condensation ran down the walls. The men were allowed only a few ounces of water a day. Haise developed a fever and a painful kidney infection. Nobody slept well. Lovell later recalled that the three of them were uncomfortable, thirsty and exhausted, but they did not turn on one another.

Then came a deadlier problem. Carbon dioxide from the crew's breathing was building up in the lander. Aquarius had filters to absorb it, but they were built for two men over two days and were soon saturated. The command module had spare filters, but they were square and the receptacles in the lander were round. On the ground, engineers gathered the things the crew had on board, including plastic bags, cardboard from a flight manual, a spacesuit hose and a roll of duct tape. They designed an adapter and read the instructions up to the crew over the radio. The astronauts built it as described, and the carbon dioxide level began to drop. It was one of the most celebrated improvisations in the history of spaceflight.

Meanwhile, Mattingly, the man who had been grounded, spent long hours in a simulator working out how to bring Odyssey back to life with almost no electrical power. Reentry required systems to be turned on in a precise order, and the power budget left no room for error. The procedure he and his colleagues devised was read up to the crew in the final hours.

Navigation was another trouble. The ship's guidance system had been shut down, and the course needed a correction. Lovell steered by hand. With no computer to tell him where to point, he lined up the Earth in his window using the line between day and night as a reference, and held the ship steady as Haise timed a burn. It worked.

On April 17, the crew prepared to say goodbye to their lifeboat. First they discarded the service module. As it drifted away, they saw for the first time how much damage the explosion had done. A whole side of the module was missing, ripped open, and its equipment hung exposed. Lovell reported what he saw to Houston, and the room listened to a description that made clear how lucky the three men were to be alive. Then the crew moved into Odyssey, powered it up, and let Aquarius go.

Reentry was the final hurdle. As the capsule plunged into the atmosphere, the heat built a sheath of plasma that blocked radio contact. The blackout normally lasts about three minutes. This time it dragged on past that, and the controllers in Houston stared at the silent screens. Many of them were afraid that the heat shield had been damaged. Then, after an agonizing wait of about four and a half minutes, a voice from Swigert came through the static. The capsule was alive.

The parachutes opened over the South Pacific and Odyssey settled into the water not far from the recovery ship, the USS Iwo Jima. The crew had been in space for almost six days. They were thinner, dehydrated and unshaven, but they were safe.

Apollo 13 never reached the Moon, but it is remembered as a success of a different kind. The explosion led NASA to redesign the oxygen tanks and add backup supplies, and the program went on to land crews on the Moon three more times. The story is still told as an example of what a team can do when everything has gone wrong. The crew had help from thousands of engineers, and the engineers had a crew that stayed calm. Together they made a failure into a rescue.
